name: The False-Consensus Effect
statement: People assume their own views and habits are far more common than they really are.
statementAccent: assume their own views and habits are far more common than they really are
meaning: The false-consensus effect is a cognitive and attributional bias in which people overestimate the extent to which their own opinions, beliefs, preferences, values, and behaviours are shared by others. We tend to see our own choices and judgments as relatively common and appropriate, while regarding alternatives as uncommon, deviant, or revealing of some flaw in those who hold them. The effect was named and demonstrated in a 1977 study by Lee Ross, David Greene, and Pamela House, most memorably in the sandwich-board experiment: students asked whether they would walk around campus wearing a sign reading Eat at Joe's split by choice, and each group estimated that most others would make the same choice they did, and judged those who chose differently more harshly. The bias distorts our sense of how typical we are and shapes how we explain disagreement, making it a fundamental feature of social perception.
mechanism: Several processes feed the effect. First, selective exposure and availability: we tend to associate with people similar to ourselves in background, values, and outlook, so our social circle is unrepresentative of the wider population, and examples of people who agree with us come readily to mind, inflating our estimate of consensus. Second, motivated projection and self-esteem: believing that others share our views validates those views, frames our choices as rational rather than idiosyncratic, and protects self-esteem, so we are motivated to assume agreement. Third, ambiguity resolution: in unclear situations we assume others see things as we do, interpreting vague terms or circumstances by our own lights and projecting that reading onto everyone. When confronted with people who choose differently, the same bias leads us to infer that they are unusual or defective in some way, since we take our own response to be the normal one. The companion false-uniqueness effect works in the opposite direction for desirable traits, where we underestimate how many others share our good qualities.

examples.text: Students asked to wear an Eat at Joe's sign each estimated that most others would make the same choice they did, and judged the opposite choosers more extremely.
Because we mix mostly with similar people, agreeing examples come easily to mind, so we overestimate how widely our views are shared.
Meeting someone who chooses differently, we tend to conclude they are unusual or flawed, since we treat our own response as the normal one.

variants.name: Selective-exposure inflation
variants.text: The mechanism by which associating with similar others makes agreement seem more common than it is across the wider population.

variants.name: The false-uniqueness contrast
variants.text: The companion bias of underestimating how many others share one's desirable abilities and traits, the opposite of false consensus for positive attributes.

whyItMatters: The false-consensus effect is a fundamental bias in social perception, attribution, and the estimation of public opinion, with wide-ranging consequences. It distorts our sense of how typical our views are, feeds overconfidence in our own positions, and shapes how we explain those who disagree, often by casting them as unusual or defective. The bias contributes to political polarisation and echo chambers, where surrounding ourselves with the like-minded inflates our sense of majority support, and it complicates efforts to gauge genuine consensus, from casual judgments to opinion polling. Its companion, the false-uniqueness effect, shows a mirror-image distortion for desirable traits. Understanding the false-consensus effect matters for recognising the gap between our perceptions of agreement and reality, for interpreting disagreement more charitably, and for appreciating how selective exposure and motivated reasoning quietly warp our picture of what other people think.

working.text: start from your own opinion or choice, which feels natural and appropriate to you.
estimate how many others agree, drawing on a similar social circle and a motivation to see your view as common.
conclude that most people share your view, and judge those who differ as unusual, overstating true agreement.

limits: The false-consensus effect is a robust and widely replicated bias, but it is a tendency, not an absolute; people do not always overestimate agreement, and accurate consensus estimates are possible, especially with good information about others. Its strength varies with the topic, how personally important or identity-relevant the view is, and the diversity of one's social contacts. The bias coexists with the opposite false-uniqueness effect for desirable traits, so the direction of distortion depends on whether the attribute is seen as good or bad. Some details of the classic sandwich-board study rest on secondary summaries rather than a readable primary text. So while the core finding, that people overestimate how common their own views are, is well established, its magnitude and direction depend on context.
misreadings: The effect is not a claim that people are always wrong about consensus; it is a systematic tendency to overestimate agreement that can be reduced with better information. It does not apply uniformly, since for desirable traits the opposite false-uniqueness bias often operates, leading people to underestimate how many share their good qualities. And it is not merely wishful thinking; selective exposure to similar others genuinely skews the examples available to us, so treating the bias as pure ego or as easily corrected by willpower alone underestimates the structural reasons our sense of consensus goes astray.
origin: Named and demonstrated by Lee Ross, David Greene, and Pamela House in their 1977 paper, including the sandwich-board experiment, as an egocentric bias in social perception and attribution.
